scenario.prompt_to_agent:
After an overnight maintenance window, pc1 (195.11.14.2) reports
pings to pc2 (200.1.1.2) are 100% lost, and pc2 reports the same
toward pc1. Yet monitoring shows the router1<->router2 eBGP
session Established with prefixes exchanged, and pc1 can still
ping BOTH of router2's addresses (193.10.11.2 and 200.1.1.1).
Identify what is dropping the traffic.

injection.action: add an iptables FORWARD rule dropping all transit ICMP

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router2 iptables FORWARD chain
Mechanism: a DROP rule for protocol icmp sits in router2's FORWARD
  chain, so any ICMP packet router2 must FORWARD (pc1<->pc2 transit
  in either direction) is discarded at the firewall layer. Traffic
  addressed TO router2 itself traverses INPUT, not FORWARD, which
  is why pc1 can still ping 193.10.11.2 and 200.1.1.1. The BGP
  session is TCP, not ICMP, so it stays Established and all
  prefixes remain exchanged -- routing is completely healthy; the
  drop is purely at the packet-filter layer.
Localization: router2
Root cause: extraneous iptables FORWARD DROP rule for ICMP on
  router2
Fix: `iptables -D FORWARD -p icmp -j DROP` on router2
scenario.fix_spec:
Remove the DROP rule on router2 -- `iptables -D FORWARD -p icmp -j DROP`.
Transit pings between pc1 and pc2 succeed again immediately; no routing or
BGP change is needed.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The failure is caused by a firewall rule on router2’s forwarding path. Control plane and L3 reachability are healthy: both routers have BGP-learned routes (router1: “200.1.1.0/24 via 193.10.11.2 proto bgp”; router2: “195.11.14.0/24 via 193.10.11.1 proto bgp”), and pc1 can ping router2’s interfaces (193.10.11.2 and 200.1.1.1), proving routing and adjacency are fine. However, host-to-host ICMP must traverse router2’s FORWARD chain, where it is being dropped.

Direct evidence on router2:
- iptables shows an explicit drop: “-A FORWARD -p icmp -j DROP” (policies otherwise ACCEPT).
- nftables confirms the same in the active ruleset: table ip filter, chain FORWARD has “meta l4proto icmp … drop” with counters incrementing (counter packets 14 bytes 1176 drop), proving in-transit ICMP is being discarded on router2.
- pc2 can ping its default gateway (200.1.1.1) but cannot ping across to 193.10.11.1/195.11.14.0/24, consistent with local INPUT allowed and forwarded ICMP denied. pc1 similarly reaches router2’s addresses but not pc2.

Localization: router2, iptables/nftables filter, FORWARD chain. Mechanism: echo-requests/replies between subnets hit router2’s FORWARD path and match the “drop icmp” rule, causing 100% loss between pc1 (195.11.14.2) and pc2 (200.1.1.2).

Root cause: An ICMP drop rule was added/left in place on router2’s FORWARD chain during maintenance.

Corrective fix: Remove or supersede the drop rule to permit ICMP forwarding (e.g., iptables -D FORWARD -p icmp -j DROP, and/or delete the corresponding nft rule), or insert explicit ACCEPTs for permitted ICMP types before any drop, and ensure persistence across restarts.
